description:
RFC 5280 §4.2 requires that a critical extension which cannot be processed MUST cause path validation to fail. Both BasicConstraints and NameConstraints are frequently critical.

cert_basic_constraints() at lib.rs:855 calls find_cert_ext (fail-open: decode errors silently become None). cert_name_constraints() at lib.rs:871 calls try_find_cert_ext (fail-closed: decode errors become MalformedCertificate).

The asymmetry is intentional (BasicConstraints is fail-open, NameConstraints is fail-closed per commit dcdc963), but the comment at lib.rs:109 in the find_cert_ext doc only says 'Use this for extensions where a parse failure is tolerable'. BasicConstraints with cA=TRUE that fails to decode would silently become 'no BasicConstraints', causing the cert to fail the 'bc.ca must be true' check at line 1755 anyway (bc is None, is_some_and returns false, NotCA error). So the fail-open is safe for BasicConstraints: a malformed BasicConstraints that can't be decoded produces the same result as an absent one — the cert is rejected as NotCA. This is acceptable.

However, this reasoning is NOT documented in the code. A future maintainer who changes the behavior of 'None from find_cert_ext' (e.g., adding a 'treat absent BC as cA=false for non-self-issued' optimization) could introduce a security regression.

Location: pkix-path/src/lib.rs:855-857 (cert_basic_constraints)

Recommendation: Add a comment explaining WHY fail-open is safe for BasicConstraints: 'fail-open is safe here because None produces the same security outcome as cA=false — the NotCA check at line 1755 will reject the cert either way. If the extension is critical and malformed, RFC 5280 requires rejection; our code achieves this as a side effect of treating None as cA=false (NotCA error). cert_name_constraints uses fail-closed because NC malformation must be explicitly flagged per RFC 5280 §4.2.'
title: cert_basic_constraints uses fail-open while cert_name_constraints uses fail-closed — asymmetry needs doc
